claims.text: Adding uniformly dispersed submicron Y2O3 particles to refractory high-entropy alloys will improve radiation tolerance.
Y2O3 modification will preserve the mechanical integrity and practical engineering properties of the alloy.
Powder metallurgy followed by optimized sintering and annealing can produce a uniform distribution of submicron Y2O3 dispersoids in an R-HEA.
Keeping irradiation temperatures below the onset of significant recrystallization will preserve the dispersoid distribution.
The introduced Y2O3 particles will form coherent or semi-coherent interfaces with the R-HEA matrix.
Y2O3/matrix interfaces will act as sinks for radiation-induced point defects.
Y2O3/matrix interfaces will act as sinks for irradiation-associated dislocations.
Irradiation-generated interstitials and vacancies will migrate to Y2O3/matrix interfaces and recombine there.
Interface-mediated defect recombination will reduce the accumulation of irradiation defects.
Reduced defect accumulation will mitigate irradiation-induced swelling.
Reduced defect accumulation will mitigate irradiation-induced embrittlement.
Y2O3 dispersoids may reinforce grain boundaries against crack initiation.
Under identical irradiation conditions, the Y2O3-modified alloy will have significantly lower defect density than the unmodified alloy.
Under identical irradiation conditions, the Y2O3-modified alloy will exhibit significantly less swelling than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will retain tensile strength and ductility comparable to the unmodified alloy after irradiation.
The beneficial effect requires a submicron, well-dispersed secondary phase within a narrow concentration window.
Excessive or poorly distributed dispersoids may reduce ductility or cause processing problems.
Analogous radiation-tolerant, dispersoid-strengthened alloys exhibit behavior supporting the proposed causal mechanism.
